warmup.q: Three settlement pods elect a leader through etcd, with a 10 s lease. The leader, pod A, freezes in a 15 s GC pause. etcd expires its lease and pod B takes over. When pod A wakes, it writes tonight's payout file. What can stop that write?
options: etcd: it revoked A's lease, so A's write fails
A's etcd client: it knows the lease expired and blocks the write
Only the payout store, if it checks a token from the election (such as the leader key's revision) and refuses one lower than it has already seen
Raft: A's term is lower than B's
warmup.why: The write goes from pod A to the payout store; etcd isn't on that path and never sees it. A's client can't help either: A checked that it was leader before the pause, and a paused process gets no signal that time passed. Only the receiver of the write can refuse it, and it needs a number that grows with every new leader to do so. Raft terms belong to etcd's own servers, not to its clients.

sections.h: Agreement is hard to build, so systems borrow it
sections.html:
Lesson 4 built Raft, and the 2015 membership bug showed how long a careful implementation can hide a mistake. Yet most systems need agreement on only a few facts. Which of three settlement pods runs tonight's batch. Which instances of the fraud service are alive. Which node owns shard 7. What the current fee table is. Embedding a consensus protocol in every service to agree on a few kilobytes is the wrong trade.

Google drew that conclusion in its Chubby paper (2006). The team built a lock service instead of a Paxos library, because application developers found a lock and a small file far easier to use correctly than a consensus protocol. A Chubby cell is five replicas running Paxos, and its clients hold coarse-grained locks for hours or days, not milliseconds. Open-source copies followed: ZooKeeper from Yahoo!, etcd from CoreOS, Consul from HashiCorp. They are called coordination services, and they share a shape. They are small: three or five nodes, the data in memory, kilobytes to megabytes. Their data changes slowly: "pod A leads settlement" changes every few minutes or hours, not thousands of times a second. And every write goes through consensus, so every change has one place in one order.

What makes them useful is four primitives on top of the key-value store, which this lesson calls the coordination instruction set:

  • compare-and-set: "create this key only if it doesn't exist", lesson 3's single decision;
  • a counter that grows with every change (the zxid in ZooKeeper, the revision in etcd), which orders all writes and makes fencing tokens;
  • sessions: a client keeps a lease alive with heartbeats, and keys tied to the session (ephemeral keys) vanish when it stops, which is failure detection;
  • watches: the service tells you when a key changes, so you don't poll.

Leader election, service discovery, group membership, partition assignment and locks are each a short recipe over these four. The figure is the picture to keep: a small consensus group in the middle, clients around it holding sessions, and the resource they protect off to one side, which is where the last check has to happen.

Agreement costs what lesson 3 said it costs. Every write is a consensus write, so adding servers makes writes slower: ZooKeeper's saturated write throughput fell from 21,000 a second on 3 servers to 8,000 on 13, while reads, served by each server from its own copy, rose. etcd's published benchmark (three members on cloud VMs) puts one client's write at 1.6 ms and its linearizable read at 0.7 ms.

sections.h: ZooKeeper: znodes, sessions and one-shot watches
sections.html:
ZooKeeper stores a tree of small nodes called znodes, named like file paths: /election, /election/n-0000000003, /config/fees. Each holds a few bytes or kilobytes. An ensemble of three or five servers replicates every write with Zab, the leader-based atomic broadcast that lesson 3 put in the same family as Raft. Every change gets a zxid, a 64-bit number that grows with each write (the leader's epoch in the high half, a counter in the low half), and every znode records the zxid that created it (cZxid), a version for its data and a version for its list of children (cversion).

Two flags on create turn the tree into coordination. An ephemeral znode belongs to the session that created it and is deleted when that session ends. A sequential znode gets a counter from its parent appended to its name, ten digits: create /election/n- three times and you get n-0000000000, n-0000000001, n-0000000002. The counter only goes up, even after the nodes are gone.

A session is ZooKeeper's failure detector. The client connects to any server and sends heartbeats. The session timeout is negotiated between 2 and 20 times the server's tickTime, which is 2 s by default, so between 4 and 40 s. The ensemble, not the client, decides when a session has expired, and deletes its ephemeral znodes then. A client that crashes without closing its session leaves its znodes in place until the timeout runs out, which the Try it shows.

A watch is a one-shot notification. Read a znode or list its children with the watch flag, and the server sends one event the next time that data or child list changes. Then the watch is gone. Between the event and your next read more can change, and a client that is disconnected misses events, so every recipe reads the state again instead of trusting the event. ZooKeeper 3.6 added persistent, recursive watches that stay registered.

Reads come from whichever server the client is connected to, out of its local copy. They scale with servers but can be stale, while writes are linearizable. A client that must see the latest write calls sync before reading.

The lock recipe from the ZooKeeper paper puts the pieces together. Create /lock/n- as ephemeral and sequential, then list the children. If yours is the lowest, you hold the lock. If not, watch only the node just before yours, and check again when it goes. When the holder dies, one client wakes up. In the naive version every waiter watches the holder, and 100 waiters wake up to find that 99 of them lost: the herd effect. In Java nobody writes this by hand: Apache Curator ships it as InterProcessMutex, and leader election as LeaderLatch and LeaderSelector. HBase and Flink's high-availability mode run on ZooKeeper, and so did Kafka until version 3.9.

try.title: Watch ephemeral nodes outlive a crashed client
steps: Start ZooKeeper (the official image is at 3.9.6) and define a helper that runs one zkCli.sh command and keeps only the interesting lines: docker run -d --name sfz-zk -m 512m zookeeper:3.9.6, wait five seconds, then zk() { docker exec sfz-zk zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 "$@" 2>&1 | grep -E '^(Created|\[|cZxid|ephemeralOwner|cversion)'; }.
Create the parent and two ephemeral sequential znodes, list them and look at one. Each zk call is a client that exits without closing its session, like a crashed pod.
Predict what ls /election shows 40 seconds later, and what name the next sequential znode gets. Then run the last three commands.

Watches: open a second terminal with docker exec -it sfz-zk zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 and type ls -w /election. In the first terminal run zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-d twice. Count the events the second terminal prints. Stop with docker rm -f sfz-zk.

code.title: in any terminal
code.html: zk create /election "" zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-a zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-b zk ls /election zk stat /election/n-0000000000 sleep 40 zk ls /election zk stat /election zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-c

try.expect:
$ zk create /election ""
Created /election
$ zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-a
Created /election/n-0000000000
$ zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-b
Created /election/n-0000000001
$ zk ls /election
[n-0000000000, n-0000000001]
$ zk stat /election/n-0000000000
cZxid = 0x4
cversion = 0
ephemeralOwner = 0x1000038624e0001
(40 s later)
$ zk ls /election
[]
$ zk stat /election
cZxid = 0x2
cversion = 4
ephemeralOwner = 0x0
$ zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-c
Created /election/n-0000000002

The two znodes outlived the clients that made them: ephemeralOwner names a session, and the ensemble keeps a session until its timeout runs out without a heartbeat. zkCli.sh asks for 30 s, so after 40 s both are gone. The parent's cversion of 4 counts two creates and two deletes, and the next sequential name is n-0000000002: the counter never reuses a number. The owner id and zxids differ on your machine. In the watching terminal you see one event, WatchedEvent state:SyncConnected type:NodeChildrenChanged path:/election, for the first create and nothing for the second: the watch fired once and was gone.

sections.h: etcd: revisions, leases and watches you can resume
sections.html:
etcd spells the same four primitives differently. It is the store under every Kubernetes cluster, and its current release is 3.7.3; 3.7 removed the old v2 API for good. Keys are flat strings, and a prefix such as /svc/payments/ plays the role of a directory. Three or five members replicate every write with Raft, through the same etcd-io/raft library lesson 4 mentioned.

The counter is the revision: one number for the whole cluster, raised by one for every change, or for every transaction however many keys it touches. Each key remembers its create_revision, its mod_revision (last change) and its version (changes since it was created). etcd is multi-version: it keeps old revisions until they are compacted, so you can read a key as it was at revision 2, and you can start a watch from a past revision. That makes watches resumable. A client that was disconnected asks for every change after revision 1,042 and misses nothing, unless compaction already threw those revisions away. ZooKeeper's one-shot watches can't do that.

Compare-and-set is a transaction: a list of comparisons, the operations to run if they all hold, and the operations to run if not. "If the create_revision of /leader is 0, which means the key doesn't exist, put /leader pod-a" is lesson 3's single decision in one line. Two pods that send it at the same moment get one SUCCESS and one FAILURE.

Sessions are leases. A client grants a lease with a time to live (TTL), attaches keys to it, and keeps it alive with heartbeats. When the TTL passes without one, etcd revokes the lease and deletes every key attached to it, and each deletion is a change with its own revision. Watches report PUT and DELETE events for a key or a prefix, in revision order and never twice. They are not linearizable, and the docs say delivery takes about 10 ms in a healthy cluster with no upper bound in an unhealthy one.

Reads are linearizable by default, served through lesson 4's ReadIndex. A serializable read is answered by any member from its own copy: faster (0.3 ms against 0.7 ms for one client in etcd's benchmark) and possibly stale. The Go client's concurrency package wraps all of this in a Session (a lease kept alive, 60 s by default), a Mutex and an Election, and etcdctl lock and etcdctl elect are built on them. jetcd, the official Java client, offers lock and election clients over the same server APIs.

try.title: Revisions, compare-and-set and a lease running out
steps: Start a one-member etcd 3.7.3 and an alias for its CLI: docker run -d --name sfz-etcd -m 512m gcr.io/etcd-development/etcd:v3.7.3 etcd --listen-client-urls http://0.0.0.0:2379 --advertise-client-urls http://localhost:2379, then alias ectl='docker exec -i sfz-etcd etcdctl'.
Write a key twice, read it with all its fields, then read it as of revision 2.
Run the same compare-and-set for pod-a and then for pod-b. Predict which one wins.

In a second terminal start docker exec sfz-etcd etcdctl watch --prefix /svc/payments. Grant a 10 s lease, register pod-a's address under it, and wait 10 seconds without keeping it alive. Keep sfz-etcd running for the next Try it.

code.title: in any terminal
code.html: ectl put /config/fx-rate 1.09 ectl put /config/fx-rate 1.10 ectl get /config/fx-rate -w fields ectl get /config/fx-rate --rev=2 printf 'create("/leader") = "0" put /leader pod-a ' | ectl txn printf 'create("/leader") = "0" put /leader pod-b get /leader ' | ectl txn ectl lease grant 10 ectl put --lease=<lease id from the line above> /svc/payments/pod-a 10.0.0.5:8080

try.expect:
$ ectl get /config/fx-rate -w fields
"ClusterID" : 14841639068965178418
"MemberID" : 10276657743932975437
"Revision" : 3
"RaftTerm" : 2
"Key" : "/config/fx-rate"
"CreateRevision" : 2
"ModRevision" : 3
"Version" : 2
"Value" : "1.10"
"Lease" : 0
"More" : false
"Count" : 1
$ ectl get /config/fx-rate --rev=2
/config/fx-rate
1.09
$ ... | ectl txn        (pod-a)
SUCCESS

OK
$ ... | ectl txn        (pod-b)
FAILURE

/leader
pod-a
$ ectl lease grant 10
lease 694da1b9e3d39309 granted with TTL(10s)
$ ectl put --lease=694da1b9e3d39309 /svc/payments/pod-a 10.0.0.5:8080
OK

and in the watching terminal, the second event about 10 s after the first:

PUT
/svc/payments/pod-a
10.0.0.5:8080
DELETE
/svc/payments/pod-a

The cluster started at revision 1, and each put raised it by one: the key was created at 2 and last changed at 3, its second version. Revision 2 is still stored, so the old value comes back. pod-a's transaction found no /leader and wrote it; pod-b's comparison failed, so its else branch read who had won. Nobody renewed the lease, so etcd deleted the key when the 10 s ran out and the watch reported it. That is service discovery's failure detection. The cluster and member ids and the lease id differ on your machine; the revisions don't.

sections.h: Leader election, discovery and locks, fenced by the revision
sections.html:
With the four primitives, the everyday jobs become short recipes.

Leader election: every candidate creates a key under one prefix, attached to its own lease. The key with the lowest create_revision (or, in ZooKeeper, the lowest sequence number) is the leader, and every other candidate watches the key just before its own. That is what etcd's Election and Curator's LeaderLatch do. Kubernetes controllers elect their leader through Lease objects stored in etcd, and every kubelet heartbeats through one.

Service discovery: each instance registers /svc/payments/<pod> with its address, under a lease. Clients list the prefix and watch it. This doesn't need linearizability. A list one second old is fine, because clients must cope with an endpoint that died a moment ago anyway, so serializable reads and a client-side cache are the right choice.

Membership and partition assignment: members register the same way, and the leader writes one key that maps partitions to members, with a compare-and-set on that key's mod_revision so that two leaders can't overwrite each other's plan.

Locks are leader election for a resource, and here the danger of the Faults, time and truth track's fencing lesson comes back. A lease only says who should hold the lock; it can't stop a holder that paused past its lease from acting when it wakes. Jepsen tested etcd 3.4.3 in 2020 and found its key-value operations strict serializable, and its locks unsafe: with 1 to 3 s TTLs, mutual exclusion failed within minutes even in a healthy cluster, and with 2 s TTLs about 18% of acknowledged updates to a lock-protected set were lost. Jepsen's answer, like DDIA's, is fencing.

Here the token comes free. The leader key's create_revision was assigned by consensus, so no two leaders share one, and every new leader's is higher. The resource stores the highest token it has accepted and refuses any lower one. Chubby called this a sequencer; in ZooKeeper the znode's cZxid does the job. The stepper plays it out with a 15 s GC pause, and the lab builds it.

One rule keeps it honest: the check must happen at the resource, in the same atomic step as the write. A payout service that checks the token and then writes in two steps has reopened the gap. In a SQL store that means one conditional statement, which the worked example shows.

try.title: Elect a leader with etcdctl, then crash it
steps: Keep sfz-etcd from the last Try it running. Each candidate runs as its own container that shares etcd's network, so docker stop is a clean shutdown and docker kill is a crash: cand() { docker run -d --name sfz-$1 --network container:sfz-etcd --entrypoint etcdctl gcr.io/etcd-development/etcd:v3.7.3 elect settlement $1; }.
Start pod-a, then pod-b. Read each one's log (elect prints the leader key once it leads) and list the keys with their create revisions.

Stop pod-a cleanly and read pod-b's log again. Then start pod-c, crash pod-b with docker kill, and time how long pod-c waits. Predict the wait first: etcdctl elect uses the concurrency package's default lease.
Clean up: docker rm -f sfz-pod-a sfz-pod-b sfz-pod-c sfz-etcd.

code.title: in any terminal
code.html: cand pod-a; sleep 1; cand pod-b; sleep 2 docker logs sfz-pod-a; docker logs sfz-pod-b ectl get --prefix settlement -w fields | grep -E '"Key"|"CreateRevision"|"Value"' docker stop sfz-pod-a; sleep 1; docker logs sfz-pod-b cand pod-c; sleep 2 date +%T; docker kill sfz-pod-b until docker logs sfz-pod-c | grep -q pod-c; do sleep 1; done; date +%T

try.expect:
$ docker logs sfz-pod-a
settlement/694da1b9e3d3930e
pod-a
$ docker logs sfz-pod-b
$ ectl get --prefix settlement -w fields | grep ...
"Key" : "settlement/694da1b9e3d3930e"
"CreateRevision" : 7
"Value" : "pod-a"
"Key" : "settlement/694da1b9e3d39313"
"CreateRevision" : 8
"Value" : "pod-b"
$ docker stop sfz-pod-a; sleep 1; docker logs sfz-pod-b
settlement/694da1b9e3d39313
pod-b
$ cand pod-c; sleep 2
$ date +%T; docker kill sfz-pod-b
23:41:50
$ until ...; date +%T
23:42:46

pod-a's key was created at revision 7 and pod-b's at 8, so pod-a led and pod-b printed nothing: it was waiting on pod-a's key. Each key is named after its lease. A clean stop revokes the lease, so pod-b took over within a second, with 8 as its fencing token. A crash revokes nothing: pod-c waited 56 s, the rest of pod-b's 60 s lease, before it led with revision 10. That wait is the price of failure detection by lease, and a shorter TTL buys a faster takeover with more false alarms. Revisions follow from the last Try it's six changes; the lease names and times differ on your machine.

video.title: Leader election with ephemeral nodes, fenced by revision

sections.h: Kafka moved its coordinator inside, and coordinators fail in partial ways
sections.html:
Until version 3.9, Kafka used ZooKeeper for all of this. Each broker registered an ephemeral znode, the controller was whichever broker created the ephemeral /controller znode first, and topic configuration lived in znodes. That meant two distributed systems to run, secure and upgrade, and a new controller had to read the whole cluster's metadata back out of ZooKeeper before it could act. Kafka 4.0 (March 2025) removed ZooKeeper; the current release is 4.4.0. The controllers now run their own Raft quorum, the pull-based KRaft dialect from lesson 4, over the __cluster_metadata log.

It is the same instruction set, built in. Brokers register with the active controller and send it heartbeats, and the controller fences a broker that goes quiet: a session. Every metadata change is a record at the next offset of the log: a revision. Brokers fetch the log as observers and apply each change: a watch you can resume from any offset. Epochs fence old leaders: a lower controller epoch or partition leader epoch is refused, as the payout ledger refused token 7. Partition data still replicates through Kafka's cheaper in-sync replica protocol, which the Messaging and logs track covers.

Coordination services fail too, and their failures spread because everything leans on them. On 2 November 2020 a switch at Cloudflare went into a partial failure for six minutes: it kept its links up but dropped some traffic. In a three-node etcd cluster, node 1 could no longer reach node 3, the leader, though node 2 reached both. Node 1 kept starting elections, node 2 kept voting for node 3, the votes tied, and no leader that node 1 could reach was elected. While elections block, Raft accepts no writes, so etcd was effectively read-only. A database cluster manager that checked the primary's health through etcd couldn't confirm it and promoted a synchronous replica, without losing data. But a defect made every replica rebuild after a promotion, and the primary of the authentication database, now without its read replicas, was overloaded. API success fell as low as 75% and the dashboard ran up to 80 times slower, for 6 hours and 33 minutes in total. Cloudflare first called it a Byzantine failure; a postscript corrects that to an omission fault. Raft's PreVote and CheckQuorum (lesson 4's Go deeper) target this kind of partial partition.

The client is part of the system as well. In 2024 Jepsen found that jetcd 0.6.0 to 0.8.2, the official Java client, retried transactions it had already sent when an answer was lost. A transaction that had committed ran a second time: updates were lost, and a conditional transaction failed its own comparison on the rerun and was reported as failed although it had committed. jetcd 0.8.5 retries only idempotent operations by default; on older versions set retryMaxAttempts(0) and handle retries yourself, with the idempotency keys you already use for payments.

try.title: Read Raft's vocabulary off a KRaft quorum
steps: From the labs folder, start the three-node Kafka 4.4.0 cluster of the Messaging and logs track (about 2.3 GB; each node is a broker and a controller voter): docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml up -d --wait.
Describe the metadata quorum's status and replication. Map each field to lesson 4's words: term, commit index, leader, followers.
Stop the node that leads (yours may not be kafka-3; change the service name, and run the next commands on a node that is still up). Predict LeaderEpoch first, then describe the quorum again.
Optional: stop a second node and try kafka-topics.sh --create. Then docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml down -v.

LeaderEpoch is the term and HighWatermark the commit index: offset 67 of __cluster_metadata is on a majority. The three voters are the Raft group, and CurrentObservers is empty because every node here is also a voter; brokers on their own would show up there. A clean stop hands leadership over at once, so describe --status now shows LeaderId 1 and LeaderEpoch 2, and the stopped node's offset reads -1. With a second node stopped, one voter is left, which is no majority, and a topic create waits about a minute and fails with a disconnect error. Offsets and the first leader differ from run to run. Output trimmed: directory ids and timestamps cut.

refs.title: Cloudflare: A Byzantine failure in the real world (2020)

analogy: A coordination service is a small notary's office for a big company. Departments don't each keep their own official register of who holds the vault key; they ask the office, which stamps every entry with the next number in its book. Anyone holding a stamped entry can prove it is newer than another. Staff who want to stay registered must call in regularly, and the office strikes off anyone who stops calling. The analogy breaks at the vault door. A real guard could phone the notary before letting someone in, but the resource a lock protects usually can't, and the notary can't stop a former key holder who doesn't know he was struck off. So the vault itself has to check the stamp number, which no office procedure can do for it.
world: Your Kafka 4 brokers already depend on a coordination layer, the KRaft controllers, and your Kubernetes clusters on etcd; both are why you run three or five of something. The pattern also shows up in your own services. A settlement or reconciliation job that must run on exactly one of three Quarkus pods needs leader election, and the payout table it writes needs a fence: store the leader key's revision in a fence row, and make every payout write a conditional update on it in the same Oracle or PostgreSQL transaction. Temporal makes a similar promise inside its own cluster, one running execution per workflow id, and its activities still need idempotency keys, the same ones you pass to the card issuer, because a timed-out activity is retried just as jetcd retried its lost answers.
mistake: The common mistake is treating a lock from etcd, ZooKeeper or a Kubernetes Lease as mutual exclusion. Teams take the lock, check that they still hold it, and then write, often with a renewal thread keeping the lease alive. It looks airtight because nothing goes wrong until a GC pause, a VM stall or a lost network packet lands between the check and the write, and then two pods both run the payout. Jepsen measured about 18% lost updates with etcd locks and 2 s TTLs. The fix is to keep the lock for efficiency and add fencing for correctness: pass the leader key's revision with every write, and have the resource refuse a lower one in the same atomic operation as the write.

compare.title: The same four primitives in ZooKeeper 3.9 and etcd 3.7

a.label: ZooKeeper
a.title: a tree of znodes, replicated with Zab
a.html:
compare-and-set  create(path) fails if it exists;
                 setData(path, data, version)
counter          zxid on every change; cZxid, version,
                 cversion per znode
session          client session, timeout 2 to 20 x tickTime;
                 EPHEMERAL znodes die with it
ordering         SEQUENTIAL znodes: n-0000000007
watch            one-shot per read; persistent and
                 recursive since 3.6
reads            local to the server (may be stale);
                 sync() first for the latest

b.label: etcd
b.title: flat keys with history, replicated with Raft
b.html:
compare-and-set  Txn: if create_revision(k) == 0 then put
                 else get
counter          one cluster revision per change;
                 create_revision, mod_revision, version
session          lease with a TTL, kept alive by the client;
                 attached keys die with it
ordering         create_revision of each key
watch            per key or prefix, from any revision
                 still kept (resumable)
reads            linearizable by default (ReadIndex);
                 serializable on request

compare.note: Both give you the same four tools, so the recipes look the same. The differences are in the details that bite: ZooKeeper's watches fire once and miss changes while you are disconnected, while etcd's resume from a revision until compaction removes it; ZooKeeper's reads are local unless you call sync, while etcd's are linearizable unless you ask otherwise. In both, the number that orders changes (zxid or revision) is what makes a fencing token.

worked.title: Fence the payout table with the election revision

steps.say: The settlement leader learns its token when it wins: the create_revision of its election key. With the Go client that is Election.Rev(); with etcdctl, read the key's fields.
steps.code: $ ectl get --prefix settlement -w fields | grep -E '"Key"|"CreateRevision"' "Key" : "settlement/694da1b9e3d39313" "CreateRevision" : 8

steps.say: Give the payout database one row that remembers the highest token it has accepted, so the check lives at the resource.
steps.code: CREATE TABLE payout_fence (id int PRIMARY KEY, token bigint NOT NULL); INSERT INTO payout_fence VALUES (1, 0);

steps.say: Every payout transaction starts by moving the fence forward, in one conditional statement. A lower token updates no row.
steps.code: BEGIN; -- 1 row: this leader is at least as new as any before it UPDATE payout_fence SET token = :token WHERE id = 1 AND token <= :token;

steps.say: The leader checks the row count before writing. Zero rows means a newer leader has written: roll back and stop acting as leader.
steps.code: val fenced = conn.prepareStatement("UPDATE payout_fence SET token = ? WHERE id = 1 AND token <= ?").use { it.setLong(1, token); it.setLong(2, token) it.executeUpdate() == 1 } if (!fenced) { conn.rollback(); stepDown(); return } insertPayouts(conn, batch) // same transaction as the fence update conn.commit()

steps.say: Replay the stepper with these numbers. Pod B (token 8) has written, so the fence holds 8. Pod A wakes with token 7: its UPDATE matches no row, it rolls back, and its payouts never reach the table. The row lock on the fence row also orders two leaders that write at the same moment.
steps.code:
fence = 8
pod A:  UPDATE ... WHERE token <= 7   -> 0 rows -> rollback
pod B:  UPDATE ... WHERE token <= 8   -> 1 row  -> payouts written

lab.title: Build a coordination service and a fenced leader election
steps: Read Coordinator.kt: sessions, keep-alives, watches and delete are provided. Everything runs on Sim's virtual clock, so a minute of leases and pauses takes a few milliseconds and every run is the same. Run the tests once: all 12 fail.

Write Coordinator.create: sequential names with nextSequence, the owning session (refuse an expired one), one new revision per create, and a CREATED event through fire. Then write expire. The five CoordinatorTest tests pass.
Write Ledger.append in Election.kt: refuse a token lower than the highest accepted, accept an equal or higher one. The first ElectionTest passes.

Write Candidate.campaign and Candidate.check, the ZooKeeper recipe: an ephemeral sequential node, lead if it is first, otherwise watch the node just before yours. The election tests pass, including the paused leader whose late write the ledger refuses.

Run everything. FencingPropertyTest runs a few hundred random minutes of pauses (up to 8 s, against a 3 s lease) and crashes: the fenced ledger's tokens never go down, while most of the same runs without the fence let an old leader write after a newer one.
hints: The parent of /election/n- is /election: use parentOf(path) and call nextSequence only for sequential creates, so /locks/n- keeps its own counter.
In expire, collect the paths first and delete afterwards: delete changes the map you would be iterating over.
In check, look your own node up again with coord.get: after a long pause it may be gone, and then you are not the leader, whatever isLeader said before.
Watch with coord.watch(path) { onWatch() }, not with check() directly: onWatch holds the check back while the process is paused, as a frozen JVM would.

drill.title: Write the election check from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write check() for a candidate that holds node, an ephemeral sequential node under electionPath: step out if the node is gone, lead with the node's createRevision as the token if it is first, and otherwise watch only its predecessor.

answer.html: fun check() { val me = node?.let { coord.get(it) } if (me == null) { isLeader = false; return } // the session expired and took the node val queue = coord.children(electionPath) // sorted by sequence number val i = queue.indexOfFirst { it.path == me.path } if (i == 0) { isLeader = true token = me.createRevision // the fencing token return } isLeader = false watchesSet++ coord.watch(queue[i - 1].path) { onWatch() } // only the one just before us: no herd }

recap: A coordination service is a small consensus group (3 or 5 nodes, kilobytes in memory, slow-changing facts) that systems use instead of embedding consensus themselves; Chubby (2006) set the pattern.
Four primitives do the work: compare-and-set, a counter on every change (zxid, revision), sessions whose ephemeral keys vanish when the client stops, and watches.

ZooKeeper: znodes, ephemeral and sequential flags, sessions timed out by the ensemble, one-shot watches, local reads unless you sync. etcd: flat keys with history, one cluster revision, leases, resumable watches, linearizable reads by default.
Leader election and locks are the lowest-key-wins recipe with one watcher per key. Service discovery is keys under a lease plus a watch, and tolerates stale reads.
No lock gives mutual exclusion on its own: a paused holder acts after its lease ends. Fence with the leader key's revision, checked by the resource in the same atomic step as the write.
Kafka 4 runs the same instruction set inside its KRaft controllers. Partial partitions (Cloudflare 2020) and client retries (jetcd before 0.8.5) are how coordination fails in practice.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a leader elected through etcd can still corrupt the payout table, and what exactly prevents it.
explain.answer: etcd elects a leader by giving each candidate a key under a lease; the lowest create revision leads, and if the leader stops renewing its lease, etcd deletes its key and the next candidate takes over. But the leader can pause, for a long GC, a stalled VM or a slow disk, between checking that it leads and writing. During the pause its lease runs out and another pod becomes leader and writes. When the first one wakes, nothing has told it, so it writes too, and two leaders have written the same batch. etcd can't stop this because the write doesn't go through etcd. The fix is a fencing token: the leader key's create revision, which consensus assigned and which is higher for every new leader. Each write carries it, and the payout table keeps the highest token it has accepted and refuses lower ones in the same atomic statement as the write. The old leader's token is lower, so its write is refused.

deeper.html:
Consul and Kubernetes leases. Consul (Raft too) offers three read modes: default, which an old leader can still answer during an election; consistent, which checks leadership with a quorum first; and stale, which any server answers and which works without a quorum, the default for its DNS interface. Kubernetes builds leader election on Lease objects in the API server, which stores them in etcd. Neither changes the fencing rule.

Watches are not a log. A ZooKeeper watch fires once and says only that something changed; etcd's watch is ordered and resumable but not linearizable, and compaction limits how far back you can resume. For a reliable stream of changes, use a log (Kafka, or a database's change data capture, which the Stream processing track covers) and keep the coordination service for coordination.

How much to trust the lease. Chubby added a lock-delay for clients that can't check sequencers: after a holder dies, the lock stays unavailable for up to a minute so that its in-flight requests drain. etcd's 3.7 release prioritizes lease revocation under overload so that leases end on time. Both reduce the window; only a fencing check at the resource closes it. DDIA's chapter 10 describes these services as a way to hand consensus to a few nodes, and lists their uses and limits.
